newsitem.title: FRANCE: Pressure mounts on Renault on closure.
newsitem.headline: Pressure mounts on Renault on closure.

text.p: Pressure mounted on French automaker Renault Thursday to reconsider closing its Belgian factory as the European Commission blocked aid to a Renault plant in Spain and workers began international protest action.
But Renault Chairman Louis Schweitzer repeated that the decision to shut the assembly line at Vilvoorde, near Brussels, with the loss of 3,100 jobs, was "irrevocable."
He said it was a tough but necessary measure to ensure the ailing company met its objective of breaking even this year.

European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert, a Belgian Socialist, said he had blocked Spanish government subsidies for a Renault plant in Valladolid, Spain, until the company changed its attitude on closing the Vilvoorde plant.

"It is of course absurd that they close a profitable company such as Vilvoorde and carry out additional investment in Spain with government aid," Van Miert told Belgian radio. European Union officials said 500 million Belgian francs (about $14 million) was at stake.
In Paris, trade union delegates stormed out of a meeting at Renault after management refused to allow a representative of the Belgian work force to address the meeting.

Some 300 workers from Vilvoorde joined 600 French colleagues in a protest march at Renault's headquarters in the Paris suburb of Boulogne-Billancourt, chanting "same boss, same battle" and "Renault solidarity."
In addition to a one-hour work stoppage in France, Spain and Belgium on Friday, the unions called a demonstration in Paris for Tuesday.

Renault SA, facing big losses and shrinking demand for its vehicles, said Tuesday it planned to cut more than 2,700 jobs in France this year after announcing plans last week to close the plant near Brussels in June.
A spokeswoman said the company might transfer some of the affected Belgian workers to factories in France.
The smallest of Europe's six car manufacturers said it has no alternative, faced with shrinking demand in France, production overcapacity and fierce competition.
Renault, which has 138,000 employees, is expected to announce a 1996 operating loss of up to 3 billion French francs ($520 million) plus major charges for restructuring. Results are due on March 20.
